1. Data funnel and how train, test and OOT were chosen

The modelling dataset keeps 580,400 of 2,260,701 loans (25.7%) and turns 151 raw columns into 61 model features, plus the target and the issue date used for splitting.

Train / test / OOT

sample rows default_rate issue_from issue_to share_60_month
train 334531 14.73% 2013-01-01 2015-06-01 8.22%
test 83633 14.73% 2013-01-01 2015-06-01 8.23%
oot 162236 14.71% 2015-07-01 2015-12-01 0.00%
  • Population: loans with a final outcome (Fully Paid = 0, Charged Off = 1) from vintages that had fully run off by the data snapshot (2018 Q4): 36-month loans issued 2013-01-01 to 2015-12-01, 60-month loans issued up to 2013-12-01. Why: in later vintages most loans were still running, and the ones already finished are biased towards early defaults and early pay-offs, so their default rates are not representative.
  • OOT (out-of-time): every loan issued from 2015-07-01, i.e. the most recent fully matured months. Why: it mimics deployment, where the model scores loans issued after its training period. It is never used for training, tuning or early stopping, so it is an honest estimate of performance on future business. It has no 60-month loans (none issued after 2013 had matured).
  • Train / test: the remaining development loans (issued 2013-01-01 to 2015-06-01) split 80/20 at random, stratified on the target. Why: test measures in-time generalisation on the same period; comparing it with OOT shows whether performance holds over time.
  • Cross-validation: 5-fold stratified CV on train only; each fold early-stops on its own validation fold, and the final model's number of trees comes from the folds' best iterations. Hyperparameter search (Optuna) also used train only.

Gain favours high-cardinality categoricals such as addr_state: the trees can split its 49 levels many ways and pick up noise. SHAP below measures each feature's actual effect on predictions and is the more reliable ranking.

3. SHAP importance (OOT sample of 20,000 loans)

Mean absolute SHAP value: how far, on average, a feature moves an individual prediction (in log-odds). Computed with XGBoost's exact TreeSHAP.

SHAP summary (feature × effect × feature value)

Each dot is one loan. Horizontal position is the feature's effect on that loan's predicted risk (right = riskier); colour is the feature's value (blue low, red high). For example, red dots on the right for dti mean high DTI raises predicted default risk.

4. Partial dependence: numeric features above 1% gain

Average predicted default probability over 5,000 OOT loans when the feature is set to each value (2nd to 98th percentile of the training data), all other features left as they are. It shows the shape of the model's learned relationship; flat curves mean little effect. Curves at the edges rest on fewer loans, so wiggles there are less reliable.

All 162,236 OOT loans, sorted into 10 equal groups by predicted risk. The bars are the default rate that actually happened; the line is the model's average predicted probability. 6. Confusion matrices at the KS threshold

The KS threshold is the score where the defaulters' and non-defaulters' score distributions are furthest apart (maximum of recall minus false-positive rate). It is set on train (0.1565, KS 0.412) and applied unchanged to test and OOT, as it would be in production. Loans scoring at or above it are predicted to default (rejected); the rest are approved.

sample tn fp fn tp recall false_positive_rate precision accuracy approval_rate default_rate_approved default_rate_rejected own_ks_threshold ks
Train 195,980.0000 89,265.0000 13,559.0000 35,727.0000 72.49% 31.29% 28.58% 69.26% 62.64% 6.47% 28.58% 0.1565 0.4119
Test 47,521.0000 23,790.0000 4,711.0000 7,611.0000 61.77% 33.36% 24.24% 65.92% 62.45% 9.02% 24.24% 0.1360 0.2901
OOT 95,719.0000 42,654.0000 9,709.0000 14,154.0000 59.31% 30.83% 24.92% 67.72% 64.98% 9.21% 24.92% 0.1288 0.2929

own_ks_threshold and ks are each sample's own optimum, for reference only; the matrices all use the train threshold. The KS threshold maximises separation, not profit: a lender would set the cut-off from the cost of a default versus the margin lost on a rejected good loan.
